2926:
Jews: the Tosefta (Yadayim 2.13) says the books of Ben Sira do not defile the hands, i.e. are not sacred Scripture, and the Talmud discusses whether reading it is permitted (Sanhedrin 100b). Yet it is quoted elsewhere in rabbinic literature as wise teaching, so its Jewish status is better described as respected but outside the canon. A common explanation is that it was known to be recent, written by a named sage after prophecy was believed to have ceased.

Protestants: followed the Hebrew canon and Jerome, who knew a Hebrew Sirach but still placed it outside the canon. Reformers also objected to lines such as almsgiving atoning for sins (Sir 3:30) and to the grandson's admission that his translation might fall short, which they took as an un-prophetic tone. Some Protestants also cite its harsh lines about women (e.g. Sir 25:24; 42:14) as reasons for caution.
2927:
Catholics, Orthodox, Ethiopians and Syriac Christians keep it. The Syriac Peshitta even translated it directly from Hebrew. It was among the books most quoted by the Fathers for moral teaching, and is listed at Hippo, Carthage, Trent and Jerusalem 1672.

Its defenders stress its antiquity (earlier than Daniel in many scholars' dating), its Hebrew original, its witness to the shape of Scripture, and its rich theology of Wisdom and the Law, which John's prologue and Jesus' invitation to the weary seem to echo. Its sayings on forgiveness anticipate the Lord's Prayer.
2928: Old Testament-era book by a named Jewish sage; apostolicity does not apply.
2929: Composed c. 180 BC in Hebrew, among the earliest deuterocanonical books.
2930: Mostly mainstream wisdom; objections centre on atoning almsgiving and some statements about women.
2931: Read across Judaism and Christianity, but formally excluded by the rabbis and the Reformers.
2932: Widely used in Jewish and Christian teaching; the name Ecclesiasticus reflects church use.
2933: The author presents his work as the fruit of study, not prophecy (Sir 39:1-8; 50:27).
2935: The Tosefta rules Ben Sira does not defile the hands, while the Talmud quotes its proverbs approvingly elsewhere.
2936: Quotes Sirach frequently as Scripture in moral teaching.
2937: Be quick to hear and slow to speak echoes Sirach 5:11.
2938: Forgive and you will be forgiven echoes Sirach 28:2.
2939: Jesus' invitation to take his yoke and find rest resembles Wisdom's invitation in Sirach 51:23-27.
2940: The parable of the rich fool parallels Sirach 11:18-19.
2941: The potter and clay image appears in Sirach 33:13 as well as in Isa 29:16 and Jer 18:6.
2953: Probably Hebrew for at least the first prose section (1:1-3:8); the poems may have been composed in Hebrew or Greek; survives in Greek and versions.
2954: Anonymous Jewish author or editors, attributing the book to Baruch son of Neriah, Jeremiah's scribe, in Babylon. Most scholars date it to the 2nd century BC.
2955:
Baruch is a short book in three parts, presented as a scroll Baruch read to the exiles in Babylon and sent to Jerusalem. The first part is a long prayer of confession (1:15-3:8) closely modelled on Daniel 9: Israel has sinned, the exile is just, and the people ask for mercy. The second is a poem on Wisdom (3:9-4:4) asking where wisdom is found and answering that God gave it to Israel as the book of the commandments. The third is a series of consolations to Zion (4:5-5:9), promising that her children will return.

Catholic Bibles attach the Letter of Jeremiah as chapter 6; Orthodox Bibles print it separately. Some details sit uneasily with history (Belshazzar is named as Nebuchadnezzar's son, following Dan 5, and Temple vessels are returned during the exile), which most scholars read as signs of a later, literary composition. The line that Wisdom appeared on earth and lived among people (3:37) was read by many Fathers as a prophecy of the Incarnation, though in context it refers to the Law.
2956: A short book written in the name of Jeremiah's secretary, Baruch: a prayer of national confession, a poem saying true wisdom is God's Law, and comfort for Jerusalem. Early Christian lists often counted it as part of Jeremiah. Catholics and Orthodox keep it; Jews and Protestants do not.
2957: Setting: Baruch reads the scroll to the exiles in Babylon (1:1-14)
2958: Confession of sin and plea for mercy (1:15-3:8)
2959: Poem on Wisdom: wisdom is the Law given to Israel (3:9-4:4)
2960: Zion's lament and consolation; the exiles will return (4:5-5:9)
2961:
Jews: not part of the Hebrew Bible; no Hebrew text survived in Jewish use, though some scholars note it may once have been read on fast days in Greek-speaking synagogues (an Apostolic Constitutions remark, uncertain).

Protestants: Jerome said he did not translate Baruch because it was not in the Hebrew, so its Latin is the Old Latin. The Reformers followed him and the Hebrew canon; they regarded the Baruch attribution as pseudonymous, pointing to the historical mismatches. It appears among the books in Article VI.
2962:
Many early lists counted Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah simply as part of Jeremiah: Origen's list (preserved by Eusebius), Athanasius' Festal Letter 39, Cyril of Jerusalem and the Laodicean canon all do so. This is why Catholics and Orthodox say it was always within the canon, not added later. Hippo, Carthage and Trent receive it.

Its confession of sin and its consolation passages are used liturgically, and the Wisdom poem is valued as a meditation on the Law as God's gift. Fathers such as Cyprian and Hilary used Baruch 3:36-38 as a testimony to Christ.
2963: Attributed to Baruch, an Old Testament figure; apostolicity does not apply.
2964: Probably 2nd century BC, though its claimed setting is the 6th century BC.
2965: Its teaching on sin, repentance and Wisdom is uncontroversial.
2966: Accepted as part of Jeremiah in many Greek and Latin lists; absent from the Hebrew.
2967: Read liturgically; quoted by Fathers as Jeremiah.
2968: Claims to be Baruch's inspired scroll; most scholars regard the claim as pseudonymous.
2969: Lists Jeremiah with Baruch, Lamentations and the Letter as one canonical book.
2970: Counts Jeremiah with Baruch, Lamentations and the Letter among the 22 books.
2971: Quotes Baruch 3:35-37 under the name of Jeremiah as a testimony that God would appear on earth.
2972: Baruch son of Neriah writes Jeremiah's words on a scroll, the background for the book's attribution.
2973: Jeremiah's word to Baruch shows his real place in the prophet's circle.
2974: Daniel's prayer of confession is the model for Baruch 1:15-2:19, often word for word.
2975: Paul's use of Deut 30:12-13 about who will go up to heaven resembles Baruch 3:29-30, which applies the same text to Wisdom.
2984: Latest likely date (before the Qumran Greek fragment)
2985: Probably a Hebrew or Aramaic original; survives in Greek. A small Greek fragment (7Q2, verses 43-44) was found in Qumran Cave 7.
2986: Anonymous Jewish author writing as Jeremiah to the exiles about to be taken to Babylon; probably composed in the Persian or early Hellenistic period.
2987:
Despite its name, the Letter of Jeremiah is a single sermon of 73 verses mocking idols. Presented as a letter Jeremiah sent to the captives going to Babylon, it warns that they will see gold and silver gods carried in procession and must not fear them. In a series of refrains it argues that idols cannot speak, see, move, save themselves from fire or thieves, or help anyone, and ends that they are no gods, so do not fear them.

Its satire builds on Jeremiah 10 and Isaiah 44 and is the kind of preaching Jews needed in a world full of images. In the Vulgate and Catholic Bibles it is chapter 6 of Baruch; in Orthodox Bibles and the Septuagint it stands alone after Lamentations. Second Maccabees (2:1-3) refers to Jeremiah instructing the deportees not to be led astray by idols, which may be an allusion to it.
2988: A short sermon, written as if from Jeremiah to exiles, mocking idols as powerless lumps of metal and wood. Catholic Bibles print it as the last chapter of Baruch. Jews and Protestants do not count it as Scripture.
2989: Introduction: the exile will be long, and you will see idols carried in Babylon
2990: Refrain-driven satire: idols cannot speak, see, defend or save
2991: The priests who profit from idols and the rites around them
2992: Conclusion: a just person without idols is better off
2993: Jews: not part of the Hebrew Bible. Protestants: Jerome excluded it (with Baruch) as not in the Hebrew; the Reformers followed, and regarded the letter as pseudonymous because its style differs from Jeremiah and it lacks his real historical detail. It is read (with Baruch) under Article VI.
2994: Origen, Athanasius, Cyril of Jerusalem and the Council of Laodicea's list all counted the Letter with Jeremiah, so Catholics and Orthodox see it as part of the received prophetic book. It is valued as a vivid, memorable teaching against idolatry that remains relevant wherever people trust in things they have made.
2995: Attributed to Jeremiah; apostolicity does not apply.
2996: Among the earliest deuterocanonical texts, attested at Qumran.
2997: Its anti-idol message matches the prophets exactly.
2998: Counted with Jeremiah in many Greek lists; absent from the Hebrew canon.
2999: Read with Jeremiah and Baruch; little separate liturgical use.
3000: Claims to be Jeremiah's letter; most scholars regard this as pseudonymous.
3001: His list of the 22 Hebrew books, as preserved by Eusebius, gives Jeremiah with Lamentations and the Letter as one book.
3002: Counts the Letter with Jeremiah among the canonical books.
3003: Jeremiah really did send a letter to the exiles in Babylon; this book imitates that act.
3004: Jeremiah's own satire against idols is the main model.
3005: The single Aramaic verse in Jeremiah, a message to the nations that their gods will perish, matches the letter's theme.
3006: Isaiah's mockery of the carpenter who worships half his log is a close parallel.
3012: Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three Young Men
3020: Probably Hebrew or Aramaic originals for the Prayer and Song; Susanna and Bel may have had Semitic originals, but Susanna contains Greek puns. Survive in two Greek versions (Old Greek and Theodotion) and later translations.
3021: Jewish storytellers and liturgists in the 2nd-1st century BC, adding to the Daniel tradition; place unknown (Judea or Egypt).
3022:
The Greek book of Daniel has three blocks of material not in the Hebrew-Aramaic Daniel. The Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three Young Men (68 verses) are inserted in the fiery-furnace story after Dan 3:23: Azariah (Abednego) confesses Israel's sins, an angel drives the flames out of the furnace, and the three sing a long hymn calling all creation to bless the Lord, still sung in churches as the Benedicite.

Susanna is a courtroom drama: two elders try to blackmail a virtuous wife, condemn her to death when she refuses them, and are exposed by the young Daniel, who questions them separately about which tree they saw her under. Bel and the Dragon contains two stories in which Daniel exposes the priests who secretly eat the food offered to the idol Bel, and kills a dragon worshipped in Babylon by feeding it cakes of pitch, fat and hair; he is thrown to the lions again and fed by the prophet Habakkuk, carried by an angel. Catholic Bibles number these Daniel 3:24-90, 13 and 14.
3023: Three sets of extra stories and songs in the Greek Daniel: a prayer and hymn from the fiery furnace, the story of Susanna saved from false accusers, and Daniel exposing the fake god Bel and a worshipped dragon. Catholics and Orthodox read them as part of Daniel; Jews and Protestants do not.
3024: Prayer of Azariah: confession in the furnace (after Dan 3:23)
3025: Song of the Three: all creation, bless the Lord (the Benedicite)
3026: Susanna: false witness by two elders and Daniel's cross-examination
3027: Bel: Daniel exposes priests eating the idol's food with footprints in ashes
3028: The Dragon: Daniel kills the serpent, is thrown to the lions, and is fed by Habakkuk
3029:
Jews: the Hebrew-Aramaic Daniel, including the copies found at Qumran, lacks these sections.

Protestants: Jerome translated them from Theodotion's Greek but marked them with an obelus as not in the Hebrew. In about AD 240 Julius Africanus wrote to Origen arguing that Susanna could not be authentic because Daniel's verdict depends on Greek wordplay (the mastic tree, schinos, and the verb to split, schisai; the holm oak, prinos, and to saw, prisai), which suggested a Greek original. The Reformers followed Jerome and the Hebrew text. Article VI lists the Song of the Three, Susanna and Bel and the Dragon separately.
3030:
The additions were part of Daniel in the Greek Bible from before Christ, and Christian art and preaching drew heavily on them: Susanna was a favourite image of the innocent saved and of the Church, and the three young men in the furnace appear in catacomb paintings. Origen replied to Africanus that the church had received these texts and that the Jews had removed passages unflattering to their elders; he also argued that puns can be imitated in translation. Hippolytus wrote the earliest surviving Christian commentary on Daniel, including Susanna.

Trent included them; the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) named Susanna and the History of the Dragon as genuine Scripture. The Benedicite is sung in Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican worship (Anglicans use it as a canticle while denying it doctrinal authority).
3031: Probably 2nd-1st century BC, slightly later than or contemporary with the final Daniel.
3032: Their theology is conventional Jewish piety: confession, praise, justice for the innocent, anti-idolatry.
3033: Universal in the Greek and Latin churches; absent from the Hebrew Daniel.
3034: Benedicite in liturgy; Susanna read in Lent in the Roman lectionary.
3035: They present themselves as part of Daniel rather than as separate revelations.
3037: Argued to Origen that Susanna was a later Greek composition, citing the Greek puns and the story's style.
3038: Defended Susanna and the other additions as part of the Scriptures used by the churches.
3039: Commented on Susanna as part of Daniel, reading it as a figure of the Church persecuted.
3040: Translated the additions but marked them as absent from the Hebrew and reported Jewish views that they were fables.
3041: The three fall bound into the furnace; the Prayer and Song are inserted right after this verse.
3042: The fourth figure in the fire is explained in the addition as the angel of the Lord who drove out the flames.
3043: Daniel in the lions' den; Bel and the Dragon tells a second, separate lions' den episode.
3044: The Song of the Three's summons to sun, moon, beasts and peoples to praise God follows Psalm 148.
3045: The law against false witnesses, which Daniel applies when the elders' testimony fails.
3054: Earlier estimate (late reign of John Hyrcanus)
3056: Hebrew original (lost); survives in Greek. Origen gives a Hebrew-sounding title, and Jerome said he had seen the first book in Hebrew.
3057: A Judean writer sympathetic to the Hasmonean dynasty, writing in Jerusalem around 100 BC about events of 175-134 BC.
3058:
First Maccabees is the main historical account of the Jewish revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes. It describes Antiochus' ban on circumcision, Sabbath and Torah, his setting up of the desolating sacrilege on the Temple altar (167 BC), and the revolt begun by the priest Mattathias at Modein. His son Judas, called Maccabeus (the hammer), wins a string of battles, retakes Jerusalem and rededicates the Temple (164 BC), the origin of Hanukkah. After Judas dies, his brothers Jonathan and Simon combine war and diplomacy to win independence and found the Hasmonean high-priestly dynasty, ending with Simon's murder and the accession of John Hyrcanus.

Written in the style of biblical history books such as Samuel and Kings, it is sober, detailed and generally regarded by historians as reliable for events, though written to justify the Hasmonean family. Notably it never shows angels or miracles, and three times says there was no prophet in Israel at the time (4:46; 9:27; 14:41), which Protestants cite as evidence that the author himself did not see his era as one of new Scripture.
3059: A history of the Jewish revolt led by Judas Maccabeus and his brothers against a Greek king who banned Judaism, around 167-134 BC. It explains the origin of Hanukkah. Catholics and Orthodox count it as Scripture; Jews value it as history and Protestants as good reading.
3060: Alexander the Great, the Seleucids, and Antiochus IV's persecution (ch. 1)
3062: Judas Maccabeus' victories and the rededication of the Temple (ch. 3-9)
3063: Jonathan as leader and high priest (ch. 9-12)
3064: Simon secures independence; the people confirm him leader until a trustworthy prophet should arise (ch. 13-16)
3065:
Jews: the book was not included in the Hebrew Bible; it was written after the period Jews regarded as prophetic, and its pro-Hasmonean stance may have made it less congenial to later rabbis, who told the Hanukkah story through the miracle of the oil instead. Hanukkah itself remained a Jewish festival.

Protestants: Jerome's rule (the Church reads the Maccabees for edification but not to confirm doctrine) and the Hebrew canon; the book's own statement that no prophet was then active; and a general Reformation conviction that Old Testament prophecy closed with Malachi. Article VI lists 1 Maccabees for reading.

Ethiopian: the Ethiopian canon contains three books called Meqabyan, which are entirely different works; the Greek 1-2 Maccabees are not part of the traditional Ethiopian list, hence n/a (debated: some modern Ethiopian Bibles mention them).
3066: It is in the Greek Bible and was counted as Scripture by Augustine, Hippo, Carthage, Trent and the Orthodox. Augustine noted that the church, not the Jews, held the Maccabees canonical because of the martyrs' endurance. Catholics and Orthodox see it as Scripture recording God's preservation of his people at a moment Daniel had foretold, and as the essential bridge between the Old and New Testaments, explaining the Feast of Dedication Jesus attended and the Jewish world of the Gospels.
3067: Written c. 100 BC, after the Jewish era of prophecy but close to its events.
3068: Orthodox Jewish piety and covenant faithfulness; no doctrinal controversy.
3069: Read in Greek and Latin churches; outside the Hebrew and Ethiopian canons.
3070: The Maccabean martyrs were venerated and the book read widely.
3071: Explicitly notes the absence of prophets in its day (1 Macc 9:27).
3072: Notes the books of Maccabees stand outside the 22 Hebrew books and gives a Semitic title for 1 Maccabees.
3073: Says the books of Maccabees are held canonical by the church, not by the Jews, because of the martyrs they describe.
3075: Used 1 Maccabees as his main source for this period.
3076: Jesus walks in the Temple at the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah), which 1 Macc 4:52-59 founds.
3077: The abomination that makes desolate; 1 Macc 1:54 uses the same phrase for Antiochus' altar.
3078: Daniel's vision of the little horn halting sacrifice and the sanctuary restored fits the events 1 Maccabees narrates.
3079: Jesus refers to the abomination of desolation spoken of by Daniel, a phrase whose first fulfilment Jews saw in the Maccabean crisis.
3080: They shall receive a little help, often read as a reference to the Maccabean uprising.
3089: Date of the first prefixed letter (2 Macc 1:9)
3091: Greek (written in Greek, with a rhetorical, emotional style).
3092: An anonymous epitomist who condensed a five-volume history by Jason of Cyrene (2 Macc 2:23), probably in Egypt or Judea; two letters from Jerusalem to Egyptian Jews are prefixed.
3093:
Second Maccabees is not a sequel but a parallel, more theological telling of events from about 180 to 161 BC, ending with Judas' victory over Nicanor. It opens with two letters urging Egyptian Jews to keep Hanukkah, then tells of the high priest Onias, the attempt by Heliodorus to rob the Temple (stopped by a heavenly horseman), the corrupt high priests Jason and Menelaus, the persecution under Antiochus IV, and the campaigns of Judas.

Its most influential passages are theological. The martyrdom of the aged scribe Eleazar and of a mother and her seven sons (ch. 6-7) contains the clearest pre-Christian statement of bodily resurrection: the king of the universe will raise us up to everlasting life. The mother's words that God made heaven and earth not from things that existed (7:28) became a key text for creation out of nothing. In chapter 12 Judas collects money for a sin offering for fallen soldiers found wearing pagan amulets, and the author praises this because he believed in the resurrection: it was a holy thought to pray for the dead that they might be delivered from sin. In 15:12-16 the dead high priest Onias and the prophet Jeremiah are seen praying for the people. The epitomist ends modestly, saying that if his work is well done that is what he wanted, and if poorly, it was the best he could do.
3094: A more dramatic, religious retelling of the Maccabean revolt, with martyr stories and the clearest Jewish statement before Jesus that the dead will be raised. It also praises praying for the dead, which is why it became a battleground at the Reformation. Catholics and Orthodox count it as Scripture; Jews and Protestants do not.
3095: Two letters to Egyptian Jews about Hanukkah; Jeremiah hides the ark (1:1-2:18)
3098: Hellenizing high priests and Antiochus' persecution (ch. 4-5)
3099: Martyrdom of Eleazar and of the mother and seven sons; resurrection hope (ch. 6-7)
3100: Judas' campaigns, Temple rededication, death of Antiochus (ch. 8-10)
3101: Offering for the dead after battle (12:38-46)
3102: Victory over Nicanor; Jeremiah prays for the people (ch. 15)
3103:
Jews: never in the Hebrew Bible; written in Greek and later than the prophetic era.

Protestants: this book was central to the Reformation dispute. At the Leipzig Disputation (1519) Johann Eck cited 2 Macc 12:43-46 in support of purgatory and prayer for the dead; Luther replied that Maccabees was not canonical and so could not establish doctrine. Calvin and the Reformed tradition added that the epitomist's apology for his style (15:38) is not the voice of the Holy Spirit, that the book praises Razis' suicide (14:37-46), and that its account of Antiochus' death conflicts with 1 Maccabees (compare 2 Macc 1:13-16 with 2 Macc 9 and 1 Macc 6). The Westminster Confession gives it no authority; Article VI allows it to be read but not for doctrine.

Ethiopian: as with 1 Maccabees, the Ethiopian canon has the unrelated Meqabyan books instead.
3104:
Catholics and Orthodox note that Hebrews 11:35 appears to allude to the Maccabean martyrs, that it was in the Greek Bible, and that Augustine, Hippo, Carthage, Trent and Jerusalem 1672 received it. They value its strong teaching on resurrection, creation from nothing, the merit of martyrdom and the communion between the living and the dead.

On 2 Macc 12, Catholics hold it shows that prayer for the dead was a Jewish practice before Christ, supporting the doctrine of purification after death; Orthodox use it to support prayers for the departed while not defining purgatory in Latin terms. They answer the modesty objection by noting that inspiration works through real human authors and styles (compare Luke 1:1-4). Augustine cited the passage in arguing that prayers for the dead are of benefit.
3105: An epitome of a 2nd-century BC history, completed in the late 2nd or 1st century BC.
3106: Catholics and Orthodox find its teaching orthodox; Protestants object to prayer for the dead and praise of suicide.
